amendments.rule: Where one Hebrew substantive is rendered by a multi-word English phrase, head it on the word carrying the lexeme rather than on the word the ASV supplies to complete the phrase. Decide which is which by dropping each word in turn: the head is the one whose loss loses the lexeme. `יַבָּשָׁה` → *dry land* heads on *dry*, because *land* alone is any land; `בָּמָה` → *high place*, *high places* heads on *high*, because *place* alone is any place; so too `קֹדֶשׁ` → *holy place*, `מִסְתָּר` → *secret places*, `תִּמֹרָה` → *palm trees*, `עֹלָה` → *burnt offerings*. **Neither part of speech nor position decides this.** The supplied word is usually the English phrase's head noun and the lexeme-bearing word usually an attributive adjective standing first, but do not move a head onto a generic noun merely because it is the noun — that reasoning would head *dry land* on *land* — and do not reach for the first word as a rule. Where the ASV supplies the modifier instead, the same test moves the head the other way: `תַּנִּין` → *sea monsters* heads on *monsters*, because *sea* is a specifier added to a word that already names the creature. **Where the subtraction test ties, read the ASV's own use of the English noun.** A class noun the ASV writes alone for a Hebrew word of that same class — in the verse, in the passage, or as its ordinary rendering of the word before you — is not a supplied generic but the word that realizes the lexeme, and a modifier standing beside it is the ASV's specifier distinguishing one class word from another, so the head stays on the class noun: JOB.4.10-11 writes a bare *lion* for `אַרְיֵה` and *the fierce lion*, *the young lions* and *The old lion* for `שַׁחַל`, `כְּפִיר` and `לַיִשׁ`, and all four head on *lion*; JOB.4.17 writes *a man* for `גֶּבֶר` and *mortal man* for `אֱנוֹשׁ`, and both head on *man*; `יֶתֶר` → *tent cord* heads on *cord*. Where the ASV never writes that noun alone for the word — *place* for `בָּמָה`, *sleep* for `תַּרְדֵּמָה` → *deep sleep* — the noun is the supplied generic and the head is the modifier, as above. Ask which of the two the English noun is before choosing, and say in the note that the other reading was available. Where the phrase also carries an article, *of*, or *a*, rules 19 and 29 place those; they are never the head. **But read whether a second source nominal stands in the phrase before sending that *of* to rule 19.** What that rule places is the relation between two nominals the Hebrew writes, and an *of* the ASV writes inside a phrase it has supplied for a single substantive is not that. Where the ASV completes the substantive with a generic head noun and writes an *of* between that noun and the word carrying the lexeme — `זָהָב` → ***things of*** *gold*, `עֵץ` → ***things of*** *wood* — the supplied noun and its *of* both join that substantive's unit, neither is `added`, and the head stays on the word carrying the lexeme, so those two head on *gold* and *wood*. This is what rule 46 already gives a bare participle or adjective in giving its supplied noun phrase *whatever article, relative or* of *the phrase needs*, holding for a substantive of any kind. Decide it by the subtraction test above: drop the English *of* and ask whether a relation between two source nouns has gone unstated, or whether only a phrase the ASV supplied for one noun has been broken in two. Where a second source nominal does stand, rule 19 governs as before and the *of* is the rectum's, whatever generic the ASV supplied to expand the first noun — `כָּל־עֵץ` → *any kind* ***of*** *tree* gives *of tree* to the rectum while `כֹּל` keeps *any kind* — and an ASV italic on the supplied words corroborates the supply and decides nothing, by rule 7. Two riders. An article morpheme standing before such a phrase takes the written *the* under rules 29 and 47, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does, so `לָעֵצִים` → *for* ***the*** *things of wood* gives the *the* to the article and *things of wood* to the noun. And a preposition the ASV writes before the whole phrase to state what it contributes to its clause is its own morpheme's, or rule 33's where no preposition morpheme stands, and is no part of the supplied expression. **A substantival numeral is such a substantive.** Where the ASV completes a numeral standing for what it counts with a generic noun the Hebrew does not write, that noun joins the numeral's unit and the head stays on the numeral, which carries the lexeme: `אֶחָד` → *one* ***portion*** in a list of tribal allotments, `אֶחָד` → *the* ***first day***. Rule 33's `added` case is the other one, and what the supplied noun does tells them apart: there the numeral is a quantity whose English is already complete and the noun names the unit it is counted in — the italic ***reeds*** after *five and twenty thousand* — so the numeral's own rendering loses nothing when it is dropped. **And a head noun the ASV supplies for a written noun to stand on as a possessive is such a completion too.** Where Hebrew writes an elliptical nominal whose fuller form names a head noun it leaves out — `אָבוֹת` for `בֵּית אָבוֹת` — and the ASV supplies that head noun, writing the source noun before it as an English possessive, the supplied noun joins the written noun's unit, is never `added`, and the head stays on the word carrying the lexeme: `רָאשֵׁי הָאָבוֹת` → *the heads of the* ***fathers houses*** gives *of fathers houses* to `אָב`, headed on *fathers*, while the construct noun and the article are placed by rule 29 as usual. Rule 18's closing sentence does not reach it: what that sentence marks `added` is a supplied *possessive* standing where no suffix or other possessive morpheme is written, and here the possessive is the very noun the Hebrew wrote while what the ASV supplies is the noun it stands on. Rule 33's supplied-phrase sentence does not reach it either, since that governs a preposition and a noun the Hebrew writes neither of, and a written noun governs this one; nor is it rule 20's supplied lexical verb, which predicates an event the Hebrew never wrote, while a head noun predicates nothing. Test by the subtraction this rule already runs: drop the supplied noun and ask whether a phrase the ASV supplied to complete one written noun has been broken, or whether what has gone is a thing the Hebrew never names at all. An ASV italic on such a noun corroborates the supply and decides nothing, by rule 7. But read what the Hebrew writes before reaching for this sentence, since the same phrase written in full is two nouns and rule 2 splits it — `לְבֵית אֲבוֹתָם` → *their fathers houses* gives *houses* to `בַּיִת` and *fathers* to `אָב` — and one chapter may write both shapes, as 1CH.26.13 and 1CH.26.21 do. The corpus places the supplied noun inside the written noun's unit, headed on *fathers*, in twenty-four units across the finished chapters and marks it `added` in none.
amendments.why: 1CH.26 marked the italic *houses* of *the heads of the fathers houses* `added` in four verses, reading rule 18's closing sentence (a supplied possessive expression is `added`) as covering a supplied head noun for a written possessor. The finished corpus does the opposite in 24 units across many chapters, including 1CH.24.6 and 1CH.24.31 in the immediately preceding chapter of the same book, keeping *fathers houses* in one unit headed on *fathers*. Rule 31 is the home for it — the supplied word completes a written substantive's English phrase — so the qualification is added where a later pass will read it, rather than left as a cross-reference that leaves the over-broad reading of rule 18 in place. The rule also states the contrast case the same chapter supplies at 26.13, where בֵּית is written and rule 2 splits the pair.

conventions: בֵּית אָבוֹת written elliptically as אָבוֹת: where the chapter writes only אָבוֹת and the ASV supplies *houses* for it to stand on as a possessive — *the heads of the fathers houses*, *by fathers houses* — the supplied noun joins the אָבוֹת unit under rule 31 and the unit heads on *fathers*; it is never `added`, and the ASV's italic corroborates the supply without deciding it. Where the Hebrew writes בֵּית itself, as at 26.13 לְבֵית אֲבוֹתָם → *their fathers houses*, rule 2 splits the pair and *houses* is that noun's own word. Settled at reconciliation against 24 corpus units, among them 1CH.24.6 and 1CH.24.31.

The chapter's directional phrases — לַמִּזְרָח, לַמַּעֲרָב, לַצָּפוֹנָה, לַנֶּגְבָּה, מִזְרָחָה, צָפוֹנָה, מַעְרָבָה, מֵעֵבֶר, בְּשֶׂכֶל — are each rendered by one English word, so the preposition fuses with its noun under rule 40 and a directive he in the phrase joins the same unit under rules 30 and 32, headed on the noun carrying the lexeme. The assimilated [הַ] MACULA segments inside such a phrase is its own `unrepresented` unit, because the one English word carries no determination; where the fused phrase is the predicate of a verbless clause the construction's copula joins that one unit (26.17 *Eastward were*), and a preposition the fusion leaves nothing to say goes `unrepresented` beside it (26.30 מֵעֵבֶר לַיַּרְדֵּן → *beyond the Jordan*).

report: Read all 45 candidate groups and the dump end to end. One real chapter-wide error, touching four verses; everything else the table flags is the ASV rendering one morpheme differently in different contexts, which the source licenses.

The error is the supplied *houses* of רָאשֵׁי הָאָבוֹת / לְאָבוֹת at 26.21, 26.26, 26.31 and 26.32, marked `added` in all four. The Hebrew writes the elliptical אָבוֹת for בֵּית אָבוֹת and the ASV supplies the head noun its written noun stands on as a possessive: that is rule 31's supplied completion of a written substantive, not rule 18's supplied possessive and not rule 20's supplied lexical verb. The corpus settles it — אָב is rendered *of fathers houses*, *of the fathers houses*, *fathers houses* and *the fathers houses* inside one unit headed on *fathers* in 24 units, including 1CH.24.6 and 1CH.24.31 in the immediately preceding chapter, and in none does the supplied noun stand outside. 26.13 is the contrast case and needs no change: there בֵּית is written, so *houses* is that noun's own word and rule 2 splits the pair. Patched in all four verses; the chapter now carries 9 `added` units rather than 13.

Determiner counting on construct chains is consistent throughout, and each shape answers to what the ASV wrote: fronting where the rectum is left with no determiner (26.12 *the chief men*, 26.15 *the store house*, 26.26 *the captains over thousands*, 26.31 *the fortieth year*); the arthrous count where a *the* stands before each word (26.19, 26.20, 26.21, 26.26 *the captains of the host*, 26.30, 26.32); a supplied *the* on the construct where no article morpheme stands (26.1, 26.22, 26.24, 26.27); and `unrepresented` where the ASV writes none (26.8, 26.17, 26.18, 26.26, 26.29, 26.32). 26.20's אֹצְרוֹת בֵּית הָאֱלֹהִים is rule 29's multi-level chain and is aligned exactly as that rule states it.

Other groups checked and left alone. בְּנֵי חַיִל and גִּבּוֹרֵי חַיִל are written both *valiant men* / *able men* (26.7, 26.8, 26.9) and *men of valor* (26.6, 26.30, 26.31, 26.32); rule 28 governs the first shape and rule 19 the second, and the difference is the ASV's. The fifteen treatments of לְ track the ASV word by word, the *had* units (26.2, 26.4, 26.9, 26.10) and 26.30's עַל → *had* alike being rule 43's verbless possessive. The copula goes to the predicate everywhere: to the preposition where the predicate is prepositional (26.8, 26.12, 26.20, 26.26, 26.29, 26.31), to the nominal or numeral predicate otherwise (26.7, 26.11, 26.19, 26.24, 26.32), and nothing is placed where the ASV writes none (26.2, 26.3, 26.22).

BSB: all 16 disagreements are documented convention differences and none is an error. The five לְ and the two other prepositions BSB represents are prepositions whose own relation the ASV leaves unstated (rule 40) — a second *to* the ASV declines to write over a coordinated member (26.16, 26.29), a לְ silenced by the מֵעֵבֶר fusion (26.30), one before a bare English object (26.10, 26.27) and one before an apposition (26.26). The seven articles are places where the ASV writes no *the* at all (rule 29's last sentence). The two waws are unrendered connectives (26.27's reordering, 26.32's relative recasting). No accepted edge was moved to improve the rate.

The two large-source units at 26.17 are preposition + noun + directive he rendered by one English adverb (*northward*, *southward*); they are genuinely indivisible under rules 30 and 32 and are left as they stand.

Considered and not changed: the impersonal *it* of 26.28, where rule 25's resumption paragraph is arguable but the referent the pronoun continues is ambiguous between the fronted כֹל and the supplied *anything*, so rule 20's `added` reading stands and the verse note already names the competitor; and 26.13's *as well ... as*, where the first כְּ takes the correlative opener and the verse note already records the reading that leaves *well* `added`.
